Projects

    

      
A project is the whole build: every input on every tab, the parts list, the OpenWAM settings and the line after the collector, the last OpenWAM results, and the dyno points and fit. Projects are kept in this program on this PC; export one to keep a copy or move it to another PC.

    Connected to Fusion. Select a sketch path, edge, tube body or keep-out body in the model, then use the Fusion tools on each tab.
  

  
Headers, collectors, crossovers, megaphones, two-stroke chambers, resonators, mufflers, catalytic converters and boom tubes, with drone, pipe vibration and turbo or supercharger tones, for anything from a single-cylinder bike to a rotary or a V12. Round, oval and flat-oval tube all work. Every figure is a first cut to build, listen to and trim; the Options tab shows what each change does.


  

    

      
      
    

    
    
    

  


  
Quick gives a whole starting build from a few answers. Simple mode hides the fine-tuning inputs on every tab and keeps their current values. Switch to Expert for every input and the full math.

Wave simulation

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        

          
          
          
          
          Used by the OpenWAM case: every runner starts at the plenum, the plenum fills through the throttle body (a step to its bore, 50 mm long) from the inlet tube, open to the air at the filter. The quick wave simulation below keeps open runners.
        

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
Enter a cam card instead (duration, lobe separation, advance)
          

            
            
            
            
          

          

          Durations as the card gives them, at 0.050 in lift on most cards (set “Cam events measured at” to match). Advance moves the intake centerline earlier than the lobe separation: a 110° cam installed 4° advanced has its intake centerline at 106° after TDC.
        

        
        
        
        
        
        
        “Match a dyno curve” under Run it in OpenWAM fills these two from your dyno numbers. The valve flow coefficient sets how freely the ports breathe (it shapes the top end); the combustion efficiency scales the whole curve.
        
        
        
        One gap per primary, in firing order, adding up to 720. A cross-plane V8 bank is 270, 180, 90, 180; a 45° V-twin into one pipe is 315, 405. Picking a stock vehicle fills this in.
        Used only by the wave simulation below the results. Valve sizes and lift are scaled from the bore, and the cam overlap from the exhaust opening above.
      

    

    

  


  
  

    

    
    

      
Engine

      

        
        
        
        

          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          
          Left: race, a bigger belly and smaller stinger for more peak power over a narrower band (Blair’s Grand Prix end). Right: broad, a smaller belly and bigger stinger for more over-rev (his enduro end). Lengths do not move; they follow the RPM and the gas temperature.
          
          
          
          
        

        
        
        
        
        The default matches Gordon Jennings's 1,700 ft/s wave speed for most of the pipe. Gas at the port runs hotter, and a hotter effective temperature makes the pipe longer.
        Blair sizes every section from the diameter of a circle with the same area as the exhaust port window: for a rectangular window, √(4 × width × height ÷ π). The gas temperature comes from the engine type: 650 °C (1,202 °F) Grand Prix, 600 °C (1,112 °F) motocross, 500 °C (932 °F) enduro.
        Lengths are measured from the port face in the cylinder bore. The port length is the stretch from the bore to the exhaust flange; the pipe you build is shorter by that much.

Tone to cancel

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        Side branches hold still gas and run far cooler than the main pipe, so they are tuned at a much lower temperature.
        

      

      
Helmholtz resonator (can on a neck)

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        The lossless curves peak at the chart’s cap. A real neck loses energy in the jets at its edges, more the louder the tone, so the peak is finite: the rows below work it out for this level (inside a running exhaust the firing tone is roughly 140 to 165 dB) with the same edge-loss K the OpenWAM line uses.
      

      
Quarter-wave tube (J-pipe) and plain chamber

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        Run the inlet and outlet pipes on into the chamber and the ring of space behind each becomes a closed quarter-wave pocket that fills the plain chamber’s pass-through notes. Munjal’s double-tuned chamber: inlet half the chamber length, outlet a quarter (the button in the results sets both). 0 is a plain chamber. In a reverse-flow chamber both tubes go in the same depth (the inlet figure) and the chamber length is from the end plate to the far wall.
        
        
      

      
Packed straight-through can, in the chamber shell above

      

        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        The core is the main pipe size, perforated, inside the chamber shell. Glass-fibre fills run about 90 to 200 kg/m³ (100 kg/m³ is about 6 lb/ft³). Set the density to 0 for a bare core, which a stainless-wool wrap comes close to. The mean flow is the gas speed in the core as a Mach number (0 for a bench test with no flow; a 1.6 L four measured Mach 0.13 at the muffler inlet at 2,500 rpm full load and 0.30 at 5,500 rpm, Liu, Hao and Liu 2012): grazing flow raises the perforate’s resistance about 1 + 72 × Mach (Rao and Munjal 1986), which is most of what a straight-through muffler does at speed.

    Method and sources
    
    
      
  • Quick build. The Quick tab runs the same formulas as the other tabs with typical inputs. Headers are tuned at peak torque RPM for low-end torque, peak power RPM for top end, and halfway between for all-round; without a torque figure it uses 70% of peak power RPM. The primary size rule picks the nearest standard tube within 8%, or the exact size. Engines with six or more cylinders in two banks get a collector per bank; four-cylinder groups get a 4-2-1 for low-end and all-round use, except on a V8, where only low-end gets one. Car primaries are capped at 42 in, since EngineLabs reports little change in the power curve between 24 and 42 in. The main pipe follows Stainless Headers’ exhaust tube sizing: about 2.2 cfm of flow per hp at about 115 cfm per square inch of pipe, with their size chart shown for comparison. The page applies that area to the inside of the tube (outside less two 0.065 in walls); the article’s own example rounds 400 hp on true duals to 2.25 in tube, which has 8% less inside area than the rule asks for, while its chart lists 2.5 in. Two more published rules are listed beside it: Dave Stadulis of SMSP’s figure of about 60 crank hp per square inch of inside area on 16 gauge tube (quoted in the article “Exhaust Scavenging”; his own table puts 400 hp on 3.00 in, so sizes within 4% pass), and the displacement-and-power chart in Nathan Morris’s Secrets of Exhaust and Intake Design (2004), which runs larger, especially for duals. The spread between them is a fair picture of how loose pipe sizing is. Without a horsepower figure, power is estimated from an assumed mean effective pressure at peak power (10.5 bar for car engines, 13 for bikes, 9.5 for two-strokes and rotaries, 1.6 times that with boost), which is this calculator’s assumption. The crossover follows Holley and Pypes (H deeper, X higher), the muffler type follows the loudness order under Muffler types, and drone lengths are the quarter-wave lengths of the drone check with 650 °F gas.
    • 
      
  • Primary length. L (in) = 850 × (180 + EVO°) ÷ RPM − 3, with EVO in degrees before bottom dead center, measured from the exhaust valve. It is a widely shared empirical formula and its constants are not derived from first principles (Stainless Headers; the same form is posted on GT40s). Stainless Headers also shows a 360 − EVO form whose worked examples plug in EVO before bottom dead center, which gives longer pipes; this calculator uses the 180 + EVO form. Use the result as a starting length, then trim on the dyno or by ear.
    • 
      
  • Runner length. The tuned length runs from the valve, the reference point Stainless Headers uses on its Tri-Y page. The tube you build is that length minus the port length from valve to flange, which you measure on your head. Lengths are tube centerline lengths.
    • 
      
  • Primary size. Area = peak-torque RPM ÷ 88,200 × displacement per cylinder (cubic inches), then inside diameter = √(area × 1.273) (Stainless Headers). The constants have no published derivation. The page lists tube sizes without saying ID or OD; header tube is sold by OD, so they are treated as outside diameters and converted with your wall thickness.
    • 
      
  • Collector. Inside diameter is primary ID × √(primaries × area ratio). The 0.8 default is a starting assumption. Burns Stainless typically uses a 15° merge and gives about 7° to 17 or 18° as the useful range, without saying whether that is included or half angle; it is drawn here as included. The makers’ catalogues now on the Parts tab add their own rules: Stainless Headers sells 13° merges for naturally aspirated, supercharged and nitrous engines and 20° for turbo (and for every 8-into-1), with a transition exit ½ in larger than the merge and 6 in long; SPD Exhaust says its 12° and 15° collectors give the largest gains while 20° and 25° save an inch or more of length, that the outlet should be no smaller than the inlet and less than twice it, that a pair of 3- or 4-into-1 collectors is “much more effective than a single 6 or 8 into one”, that its 3°, 7° and 13° transition cones handle steps of ½, ¾ and 1 in, and that open headers want a reverse cone; Burns wants the exit larger than the throat (an hourglass) and a megaphone plus reverse cone on open headers. These are makers’ experience, not published tests, and they bracket the 15° default here rather than change it.
    • 
      
  • Collector rules. Collector diameter 1.75 to 2.00 times the primary diameter and collector length 0.5 times the primary length (Stainless Headers). The source does not say ID or OD, and its examples use nominal tube sizes, so the check compares outside diameters. It does not say how many primaries either; the check is only shown for four per collector.
    • 
      
  • Megaphone. Length is (exit ID − inlet ID) ÷ 2 ÷ tan(included angle ÷ 2). Gordon Jennings found an 8° divergence most efficient at recovering pulse energy (Cycle World, 1964). The warning above 14° is this calculator’s threshold, not a published one.
    • 
      
  • Expansion chamber. Tuned length is exhaust duration × c ÷ (12 × RPM), from the port face to the reflection point. Jennings used a 1,700 ft/s wave speed for most of the pipe and tuned to the midpoint of the convergent cone (Cycle World, 1964), so the default effective temperature gives about 1,700 ft/s. Stinger 0.59 to 0.63 of header diameter and 12 diameters long, diffuser 7° to 9°, baffle 16° to 25° (Wikipedia); the formulas from Jennings’s Two-Stroke Tuner’s Handbook, as summarized in “How Two-Stroke Expansion Chambers Work,” give a stinger 0.58 to 0.62 of the header, a diffuser of 7° to 10°, a baffle of 14° to 20° at about twice the diffuser angle, and a header 10 to 15% larger in area than the port, so the notes use the combined ranges. The same summary notes that some measure from the port and some from the cylinder center, and that the reflection point is taken at the center of the baffle cone counted out to its virtual tip, which sits a little past the middle of the cone you build; that is why the reflection point is an input. The belly ratio is a design choice; Jennings’s 1964 example opened to about six times the header area. Lengths run from the port face in the bore, so the port inside the cylinder counts as header. The Blair option follows Gordon Blair’s two-stage diffuser chamber (Design and Simulation of Two-Stroke Engines, SAE 1996), from the same summary: tuned length = 83.3 × speed of sound × exhaust duration ÷ RPM, in mm, from the piston face to the start of the stinger; an average exhaust temperature of 650 °C for Grand Prix engines (about 11 bar mean effective pressure), 600 °C motocross (9 to 10 bar), 500 °C enduro (8 bar) and 350 °C road bikes (5 bar); sections of 10, 41, 14, 11 and 24% of the tuned length, with a stinger as long as the baffle; and diameters of K1, K2 and K0 times the port’s equivalent diameter (1.05, 3.25 and 0.6 Grand Prix; 1.125, 2.25 and 0.7 enduro; motocross K0 0.65), with the second diffuser starting at (41 ÷ 55)1.33 of the belly diameter. Blair gives no motocross K1 or K2, so this page takes the midpoint of the other two, and none for road bikes, which therefore appear only in the tuned-length check.
    • 
      
  • Speed of sound. Exhaust acoustics (resonances, branch and chamber lengths, wave travel times) use burned-gas properties: c = √(γ R T) for stoichiometric gasoline exhaust, γ from the NASA (GRI-Mech 3.0) heat capacities of its CO₂, water, nitrogen and argon, R 286.6 J/kg K, about 2 to 4% below air at exhaust temperatures. Intake air, and the empirical rules whose constants were set with air (Blair’s class temperatures, the 2-stroke default tuned to Jennings’ 1,700 ft/s), keep air’s c = 20.05 × √(temperature in kelvin).
    • 
      
  • Stepped primaries. Each section is 1/8 in (3.2 mm) larger, taking 50/50 or 50/25/25 of the tuned length (Stainless Headers). Most stepped headers use sharp steps, and smooth transitions are needed on very thin wall, 0.035 in or less (PRI), so the default is a sharp step and a transition cone is optional. The RPM listed for each step applies the primary-length formula to the distance from the valve to the step; it is an estimate, not a published rule.
    • 
      
  • Resonance chambers on the header. A sealed can or a shell around the pipe on bleed holes is treated as a Helmholtz side branch: the volume is the can, or the space between shell and pipe, and each hole’s effective length is the wall plus 0.85 × its diameter, the usual allowance for a hole flanged on both sides. Its sound curve and 3 dB band use the same side-branch formula as the Mufflers tab, and the hole size for a chosen tone solves the same equation backwards. An inline bulge uses the plain-chamber formula, and the share of a pulse it sends back is (1 − area ratio) ÷ (1 + area ratio) (Parker, Imperial College). Gas in the chamber defaults to the header temperature. What makers and testers report: Kawasaki, KTM via Motocross Action, Motocross Action’s chamber guide, Dirt Rider on the Megabomb, FMF on the Powerbomb, Dirt Bike Test on Pro Circuit’s RC-4 and the Buell patent application. None publishes dyno curves, so the page does not predict a power change.
    • 
      
  • Wave simulation. Each cylinder breathes through its own intake runner and the 4-Stroke tab’s header. With more than one primary per collector, every cylinder on that collector is modeled: the primaries meet at the start of the merge cone, which opens at their combined area, and fire at even spacing or at the gaps you enter, so a cross-plane V8 bank’s 90° pair shows up as one cylinder filling worse than the others. The meeting point is solved like the two-pipe junctions, with one pressure shared by every branch and the inflows mixed; a small wave arriving there from one primary splits as linear acoustics says, within 0.3% of the textbook share. Collectors run on a 12.5 mm grid, which gives the same torque as the 10 mm grid within about 0.5%. Each pipe solves the one-dimensional compressible flow equations with area change, wall friction and Reynolds-analogy heat transfer, using a MUSCL-Hancock finite-volume scheme and an HLLC Riemann solver. Sudden size changes are joined by characteristic junctions, sealed chambers are lumped volumes on an inertial hole neck, pipe ends open to still air, and valves are compressible orifices with a 0.7 discharge coefficient and sin² lift. The cylinder is a single zone with a Wiebe burn (18° before top center, 55° long, air-fuel 12.8), Woschni wall heat loss, and 72% of the fuel heat kept in the gas, a calibration that brings full-throttle torque into the range of real engines. A fresh-charge tracer sets the trapped air. Checks run here: the Sod shock tube matches the exact solution within 0.4%, small waves at a fourfold step split −0.60 and 0.40 as linear theory says, a wave at an open end comes back inverted at about −0.96, and halving the grid moves torque by under about 2.5%. It has not been checked against a dyno, so use it to compare designs, not to predict horsepower. Designs are compared at each speed and by their average over the range, the area under the curve that a Formula SAE team used to rank its intakes (SAE 2003-01-2277); that team also found that resonance formulas only predict a range and finished the plenum on the dyno.
    • 
      
  • Reference books and papers. Besides the links above, these were read for this page: the nsxprime “Exhaust Theory” FAQ (a Burns Stainless article on collector reflections, a pipe material table, and a Pontiac 3-tube against 4-tube header test), “Exhaust Scavenging” (the Davis back-pressure test and SMSP sizing), “How Two-Stroke Expansion Chambers Work” (Blair and Jennings), Nathan Morris’s Secrets of Exhaust and Intake Design, SAE 2003-01-2277, Potente (Acoustics 2005), Liu, Hao and Liu 2012, Mohammad et al. 2017, Bönnen et al. 2016 and MacInnes’s Turbochargers.
    • 
      
  • Tri-Y (4-2-1). The first section defaults to 14.5 in, inside the 13 to 16 in range, and the secondary is the tuned length minus the first section. The same page gives about half the tuned length as a separate guideline for the second merge (Stainless Headers). It gives no secondary size; 0.8 of the two primaries’ area is this calculator’s default. Pairs keep the closest pulses as far apart as possible: 1 with 4 and 2 with 3 on an inline-4 at 360°, and 270°/450° on a cross-plane V8 bank (Wikipedia). A check on a 1,627 cc Toyota 4A-GE with 300°+ cams and 52 mm individual throttles, on a dyno with a straight-through test muffler (Garage 4age, 4-2-1 vs 4-1): with the secondary (Y to collector) cut from 1,250 mm down to 400 mm, 500 to 700 mm was best, the gain all below about 6,000 RPM and the top end (about 150 hp near 9,500) the same; at 1,250 mm the torque fell into a hole near 4,500 to 5,000 RPM, less so at 1,100 mm, and at 400 mm the bottom end got worse. This calculator’s rule gives a 491 mm secondary for a 6,000 RPM tune on that engine (80° EVO), in that window.
    • 
      
  • 180° and 8-into-1. A cylinder’s pulse angle is its place in the firing order × 720° ÷ cylinders. Every other cylinder in the firing order gives each collector a pulse every 180° on a V8 (Motorstate). These spacings are worked out from the firing order. An 8-into-1 puts every pulse in one collector, 90° apart on a cross-plane crank, so the firing frequency dominates and the exhaust loses the bank rhythm that makes duals burble. The worked example in the Headers notes is a Swartz Garage study of an LS7 Ultima GTR (1.75 in primaries stepped to 1.875 in at 18 in, about 39 in long, 4 in outlet, 4 × 6 in resonator) with Greg Holman’s rules: step the primary when it runs past 36 in, start at 1.75 in naturally aspirated or 1.875 in supercharged, keep any muffler near the tip because a long pipe after it turns raspy; and SPD Exhaust’s note that two outlets are fine because the 8-into-1 sets the sound. Its dyno clip was reviewed with the AI video model: no numbers on screen, and the sound is a smooth, high-frequency, racing-engine shriek rather than a muscle-car rumble, which is what the even 90° spacing predicts. Those pipe sizes are one builder’s choices, not a measured optimum; the calculator sizes from displacement and RPM as usual.
    • 
      
  • Fit to your space. A runner shorter than ideal is converted back to the RPM it tunes for with the same formula. A collector that is too short keeps its merge cone and loses straight length first, then tries an 18° merge, the steep end of Burns’s range. A collector OD limit is converted to the area ratio it leaves.
    • 
      
  • Intake. Airflow is displacement × RPM × volumetric efficiency × boost pressure ratio; K&N’s rules (filter area = cu in × RPM ÷ 20,839 in²; airflow = cu in × RPM ÷ 3,456 cfm; a round filter flows diameter × height × 6 × π cfm and a panel length × width × 6) are from GNTType, with K&N’s permission. The 180 ft/s air-speed limit, the runner wave formula and the ram tube rule are from Grape Ape Racing’s “Induction Pressure Wave Tuning”; Vizard’s and Magnante’s runner rules and Thompson’s tube-to-throttle area of 1.25 to 1.33 come from the “Intake Pulse Calculation” article. Duct loss is Darcy friction (Haaland), 0.2 velocity heads per smooth 90° bend (Crane Technical Paper 410 gives about 14 friction factors for a bend of 1.5 diameters radius), and the inlet’s vena contracta loss (1/Cd − 1)² with Blair and Cahoon’s discharge coefficients (plain 0.567, radius 0.719, elliptical 0.743); their best bellmouth is one exit diameter long, 2.13 exit diameters across the entry, with a lip radius of 0.08 entry diameters. The power change uses the SAE J1349 correction factor, 1.18 × (99 ÷ Pd) × √((T + 273) ÷ 298) − 0.18, between the outside air and the air at the filter; Racing Beat’s 1% per 10 °F agrees within a few tenths. Induction resonances: a tube between open air and the plenum is a Helmholtz neck on the plenum (half the displacement when not given) plus half-wave modes; an airbox and snorkel is a Helmholtz resonator with the 0.6133-diameter neck correction. The loudness order of airbox, open filter and individual throttles is general practice, not a measurement. Induction sound: the mouth’s end correction by its type (open tube 0.6133 × radius, Levine and Schwinger 1948, as in Morse and Ingard, Theoretical Acoustics, 9.1; a flared mouth as a flanged opening, 0.85 × radius, Rienstra and Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics, 4.4.3; horn loading, Kolbrek, NTNU thesis 2016); the edge-tone whistle rule (Strouhal 0.2 to 0.3 on the gap, Rienstra and Hirschberg 4.4.3 and fig. 4.9; Angster, Rucz and Miklós, Acoustics Today 2017 on organ flues); resonators in parallel (Calton and Sommerfeldt, BYU).
    • 
      
  • Crossovers. H-pipe diameter defaults to 0.8 of the main pipe, in line with Holley’s examples (a 2.0 in tube on 2.25 to 2.50 in pipes, 2.25 in on 3.0 in). Holley puts the crossover 8 to 18 in from the collector ends, says only sound waves and pressure differences pass through an H-pipe, and describes the H as deeper and the X as higher pitched, as does Pypes. The X-pipe angle and merge length, Y-pipe angle and Z-pipe jog angle are this calculator’s defaults. The X-pipe build sheet lists every bend, leg and miter for the angle you enter and shows what other angles would do; the shared opening is the length over which two crossing tubes intersect (diameter ÷ sin of the angle, plus any merged section). Burns Stainless is reported to recommend about 15° for an X (LS1Tech thread); no maker publishes test data on X angle or merge length. The only Z-pipe found is a 3D-printed mid-engine part whose internal shape is not published (Ace Race Parts), so the Z-pipe gives geometry only.
    • 
      
  • Drone and pulse tones. Each pipe’s tones come from the spacing of the pulses that reach it, treated as an ideal pulse train: even spacing gives the firing tone and its multiples, and a cross-plane V8 bank’s 90/180/270/180° gaps add half-order tones. The roll-off used to rank higher tones is this calculator’s simplification. The pipe is treated as closed at the valves, or at the turbine, and open at the tip, so resonances fall at (2n − 1) × c ÷ (4 × length). Mufflers and diameter changes shift real resonances, so use this as a screen and confirm with a recording. The same check runs at idle for strong and moderate tones: with a rear muffler, the lowest mode is the tailpipe gas bouncing on the muffler’s gas, a resonance Faurecia’s engineers say commonly falls on the firing frequency at idle or low speed (Bönnen et al. 2016).
    • 
      
  • Packed mufflers. The packed straight-through can on the Mufflers tab is a perforated core inside a closed shell: plane waves in the core and in the packed annulus, coupled through the perforate, are carried along the can as a 4 × 4 transfer matrix (the Sullivan and Crocker form) with the annulus ends rigid and no mean flow. The packing comes from Antebas, Denia, Pedrosa and Fuenmayor 2013: flow resistivity R = 1.316074 × density^1.782163 for texturized glass roving, their Delany-Bazley-type fits for the fibre’s impedance and wavenumber against f × ρ₀ ÷ R, and the perforate impedance [0.006 + j k (t + 0.425 d (1 + Zₘkₘ ÷ Z₀k₀) F(σ))] ÷ σ with F the mean of Ingard’s and Fok’s corrections. With the packing removed and the core open the model reproduces the plain-chamber curve to within half a decibel up to 1 kHz, which is the check that the coupling is right; with packing it shows their trends, more loss at mid and high frequency with density and with porosity. It is plane-wave only, so it is drawn to the shell’s first cross mode (0.586 c ÷ D, from Joseph’s duct acoustics lecture, j′₁₁ = 1.8412), and capped at 40 dB because real cans flank. Two weaker sources were read alongside and not coded: a transfer-matrix conference paper (Abdullah et al., UTM) whose claims that a baffle farther from the inlet and a thicker baffle give better attenuation come with no physics, a thicker baffle being just a longer neck; and a simulation-only muffler study of a KTM 390 (Saadabadi et al. 2023) whose mass-flow input, 0.163 kg/s, counts every stroke as exhaust and uses the wrong density, about five times the real flow, so its back-pressure figures are not used, only its design ranking (short fat chambers, centred baffle holes, extended inlet and outlet tubes). Plug (cross-flow) muffler. The same coupled equations with Munjal’s boundary conditions for the cross-flow expansion and cross-flow contraction elements (Acoustics of Ducts and Mufflers, 1987, 3.8.1, Fig. 3.10b–c, eqs. 3.120 and 3.122 with the end pockets closed): the inlet tube plugged at the end of its perforate, the shell closed behind each perforate, a plain annular duct between the two, and Sullivan’s cross-flow perforate impedance (eq. 3.153, [0.514 d₁M ÷ (lσ) + j 0.95 k₀ (t + 0.75 d_h)] ÷ σ, the stationary 0.006 ÷ σ resistance with no flow). Checked by its limits: it is finite and positive across the band, the flow through the holes raises the loss everywhere, and a perforate longer than half the shell is refused. The mean flow is kept out of the wave equations, as in the packed can, so the convective shift of the peaks is not shown; Munjal (8.3) puts a cross-flow element’s back pressure at 2 to 4 dynamic heads against under 1 for a plain chamber, which the tab reports.
    • 
      
  • Davies 1996. P. O. A. L. Davies, “Piston Engine Intake and Exhaust System Design,” Journal of Sound and Vibration 190(4), 677 to 712, is the source of the layout rules on the Mufflers tab: side-branch length c ÷ 4f for the lowest band, a set of branches stepped by 3^(−1/m), the folded branch l = Xᵢ + (Sₒ ÷ Sᵢ) Xₒ with its 10 to 15 × chamber area and 0.5 d and 1.5 d gaps, the 20 log (chamber ÷ pipe area) swing between peaks and holes, the open-end correction 0.6133 − 0.1168 (ka)² and 0.6393 − 0.1104 ka, the step-in correction 0.63 a (1 − e^(−(a₂/a₁ − 1)/1.5)), 3 mm holes at 10% open as the perforate compromise, and the point that a perforate is nearly transparent above 15% open at low flow speeds. Not carried over: his small-car example where halving back pressure gave about 20% more peak power, far above what Bell or Heywood would expect and clearly a very restrictive baseline, and his truck and ship numbers, which are one-off designs.
    • 
      
  • Yasuda 2013, Elsayed 2017, Xie 2015. The production muffler check uses Yasuda et al.’s lumped formulas for the low-pass cut-off, the return-pipe resonance and the interconnecting-hole Helmholtz dip with end corrections 0.61 d (open pipe) and 0.85 d (hole), the 5 × to 12 × displacement volume rule, and their guidance on equal chambers and a long tailpipe; run on their own specimen the formulas land within about 10% of their resonances. The baffle rules from Elsayed et al. and the built-in resonator fix from Xie are quoted in the muffler types list, not computed; both are simulation studies validated on one geometry.
    • 
      
  • Sporty exhaust sound. The lean on the Sound tab’s four-cylinder note takes the regression weights of Yang, Jia, Liao, Zhang and Chu 2024 by rpm band (order 2: −0.041, −0.034, −0.026; order 4: +0.018, +0.015, +0.022; order 6: +0.026, +0.023, +0.014 per dB(A); intercepts 6.7, 6.6, 6.1) and applies them to the page’s pulse-train orders, A-weighted and relative to order 2, so only the balance between orders is scored. The study used 52 jurors on 30 economy cars at full throttle with orders raised by 8 dB in a factorial design; its CNN scoring model is not needed here. It is one engine class and one study, so the page calls the result a lean, not a score.
    • 
      
  • Cone Engineering. Four of the maker’s tech sheets were read. Taken: the collector area-growth table, (D out ÷ D in)² − 1 with its bands (4-1 naturally aspirated 100 to 150%, drag to 200%; 3-1 about 100% or less; 2-1 motorcycle 50 to 75%; two car headers into one 30 to 50%; Tri-Y steps 15 to 30%), now on the Headers tab next to the 0.8 area-ratio result, computed on inside diameters where the table uses nominal sizes; the 2007 Bonneville test of six exhausts (peak 58.0 to 65.3 hp, dB at 2 and 50 ft, time to power), shown on the Mufflers tab for motorcycles; and their fabrication rules, start from the stock header’s inside diameter because many stock headers are double-walled, 16 gauge as the common wall, mild steel runs cooler than stainless unless ceramic coated inside and out. Treated as opinion: that packing adds nothing in motorcycle-size cans and a stainless-wool wrap is enough, which Davies and Antebas contradict; that velocity is the key to sound and scavenging; and the sound figures themselves, which the authors call unscientific. The collector table disagrees with Sanderson’s 1.75 × diameter rule (+206%, Fast Ford, April 2007), and with this page’s own 0.8 × 4 default (+220%); both are shown rather than reconciled.
    • 
      
  • Hobby and forum sources. Grape Ape Racing’s intake pages, the team-integra runner-size blog, Paul Lamar’s rotary intake notes and Jim McFarland’s Enginology column were read for anything the textbooks miss. Kept as quick estimates only, since Engelman’s model on the Intake tab supersedes them: Vizard’s 7 in at 10,000 rpm plus 1.7 in per 1,000 rpm, Magnante’s N × L = 84,000, the plenum volume rules (four-cylinder 50 to 60% of displacement, V8 40 to 50%, smaller for high rpm), port area 78 to 80% of the valve head, taper 1.7 to 2.5% area per inch, and McFarland’s alternating-cylinder tuning. Rejected: the claim of 10 psi at the intake valve in a tuned system (measured peaks are 3 to 5 psi); the “180 ft/s” diameter formula used as a per-runner rule, which is a whole-engine, cycle-averaged velocity and sizes a single throttle or plenum inlet, while Engelman’s 200 ft/s is the mean speed in one runner during its 180° stroke, about four times higher; the statement that throttle bodies without a plenum lose all resonance; and the inconsistent 1.25 against 1.33 intake-tube area factor, where the worked example fits 1.25.
    • 
      
  • Two-stroke paper and the lecture slides. A 2018 polytechnic paper (Ismail et al., Politeknik Sultan Mizan Zainal Abidin) re-applies Blair’s empirical expansion-chamber proportions and confirms the constants already on the Two-Stroke tab, including that the third section is 0.14 of the tuned length where its text misprints 0.41; its dyno tables, which show negative brake power “from back pressure” and peak power at 3,500 rpm on a 108 cc engine, and its exhaust temperatures (road racing 450 °C, enduro 300 °C against Blair’s 650 and 500) are not used. A 2025 induction and exhaust slide deck reproduces Heywood’s and Stone’s valve-size tables and a ValveFlow.m check case (100 × 100 mm, CR 10: VE 0.95 at 2,000 rpm, 0.89 at 4,000 rpm); only its text layer could be read, its tables are to be verified against the originals before use, and its statement that the exhaust critical pressure ratio is “about 3” because of the lower gamma is wrong, a lower gamma moves the ratio toward 1.8 (1.86 at γ = 1.35), though the cylinder-to-port ratio at opening is often above 3.
    • 
      
  • Airbox CFD and the Clemson proposal. Andrews and Srinivasan 2015 (CFD on a production airbox) report pressure-drop cuts of 33% from a mesh and bell-mouth at the inlet, 28% from baffles under the filter and 22% overall; those are kept as the size of gain a clean airbox path offers, while their “10 to 20 horsepower” is unsupported by any engine test and is not repeated. A 2011 Clemson course proposal is used only for the magnitudes it cites from Sammut and Alkidas (SAE 2007-01-0492): intake length tuning worth up to +12% volumetric efficiency and exhaust length up to +5%, independent and additive at full throttle, with pressure at intake closing up to 1.25 × the untuned value. The Auto Math Handbook’s airflow chapters (cfm = rpm × cu in ÷ 3,456, hp = BMEP × cu in × rpm ÷ 792,000, Urich’s volumetric-efficiency classes, the SAE J607 correction) add nothing the page does not already compute.
    • 
      
  • Resonators. Helmholtz frequency is c ÷ 2π × √(neck area ÷ (volume × (neck length + 0.6133 × neck diameter))), with the end correction and the side-branch transmission-loss formula from Southampton, APAC 2018 (after Möser and Selamet), used here in its lossless form. That form gives a 3 dB band of K × the target frequency, where K = √(neck area × volume ÷ effective neck length) ÷ (2 × pipe area). A J-pipe is c ÷ (4 × frequency) long (Stainless Headers), less this calculator’s allowance of 0.3 × its diameter for the open end. Stainless Headers measured a branch at about 90 to 110 °F at cruise, so side branches are tuned at the resonator temperature, not the exhaust temperature. Real resonators peak lower and broader than these lossless curves, which the chart caps at 40 dB.
    • 
      
  • Fabrication jigs. The Fusion panel on the Headers, Intake, Mufflers and Parts tabs builds 3D-printed fixtures under the tubes the last auto-route built (or selected centrelines), cut to the tube outside diameter plus a clearance and open at the centreline so each piece drops in and lifts out. Five styles: separate cradles; cradles tied into one frame by ribs along the shortest tree between their feet; a plate following each tube with its cradles, bridged between tubes; continuous saddles broken at every weld joint between the cut pieces (the torch’s room) and split to the print bed; and a flange frame of locator plates (bore and bolt circle) at the free tube ends joined by beams. Layout as drawn, or laid flat on the part’s widest side (the normal of the best-fit plane through its centrelines), which on the test Tri-Y header cut the tallest part from 635 to 171 mm. Free-standing parts get feet that grow with their height (0.5 × along the tube, 0.6 × across); on a fixture table, bolt holes go on its grid (System 16: 50 mm pitch, 16 mm holes; System 28: 100 mm, 28 mm; 5/8 in on 2 in; or any) only where a foot, rib or tab has a rim round them and a bolt head clears the blocks, with tabs out to the nearest grid holes where a part has too few. Cradles step a block and a weld gap off the joints; parts bigger than the bed are listed.
    • 
      
  • Timbre tube bundle. Borla’s “timbre scaled exhaust system” (US 10,808,584 B2, David Akiba Borla, priority 25 July 2016; continuations US 11,661,870 B2 and US 12,037,930 B2, EP 3 488 087 B1) claims 3 to 5 parallel, unperforated tuning tubes of 1 to 1.5 in diameter and about 1 to 8 in length between an inlet and an outlet collector, in line ahead of the muffler or on each side of a dual system, the outer tubes longer, each tube’s diameter and length chosen from the vehicle’s root note for a desired note. The patent gives no formula. The Mufflers tab models the bundle with plane waves: each tube a lossless duct with 0.3 × its diameter added at each collector, the collectors as point junctions, the tubes’ admittance matrices added in parallel and the result turned back into a transfer matrix for the transmission loss between equal pipes. It reproduces the two-path Herschel–Quincke notch at c ÷ (2 × the length difference). Tubes this short resonate in the kilohertz range, so the bundle changes the harmonics of the note (its colour), not its pitch; the tab can size the tubes so their half-wave resonances land on chosen harmonics of the firing tone.
    • 
      
  • Spiral sound traps and auger mufflers. The spiral trap inside a Spintech (a wall bent a little over one turn standing across the case, the main flow crossing its opening, vents in its back face drawn out by the venturi between the trap and the case wall, no packing) is the design of US 5,824,972 (Boyd L. Butler, filed 1997); Spintech says only that its “spin sound trap” is patented, so the link is the match of the design, not a confirmed assignment. The patent compares, at 2½ in inlet and outlet and 5 in of water: friction mufflers 13 to 20 dBA at 70 to 100 CFM, straight-through absorption 2 to 7 dBA at about 200 CFM, the spiral traps 8 to 15 dBA at about 175 CFM. The Mufflers tab scales those with inlet area and the square law (drop ∝ density × flow²) to this engine’s redline flow, and lists Spintech’s case sizes against the space limits (case size chart). Auger mufflers (the Lobak, by forum accounts later Moroso’s; the Moroso Spiral Flow; the design of US 3,963,092, Soares, 1976) wind a helical baffle round a straight centre tube; the tab models the tube and the helical channel (N √((π Dm)² + p²) long) as two parallel paths with the same transfer matrices as the tube bundle. No maker data for the Lobak was found; Moroso claims 5 to 7 dB and 850 CFM with no method.
    • 
      
  • Plain chamber. Transmission loss is 10 log [1 + ¼ (m − 1/m)² sin²(kL)], with m the area ratio and L the chamber length; it drops to zero wherever the chamber is a whole number of half waves long (Wikipedia). The formula assumes plane waves, which a round chamber carries only below its first cross mode, at k × radius = 1.8412. Potente (“General Design Principles for an Automotive Muffler,” Proc. Acoustics 2005, Australian Acoustical Society) recommends a chamber at least 1.5 times as long as its diameter, inlet and outlet extensions at least 1.5 chamber diameters apart, and notes that a bigger expansion ratio gives more loss; a GT-Power study of a 15 L muffler on a 1.6 L engine found a bigger shell quieter and trusted its plane-wave model only to about 1 kHz (Mohammad et al. 2017). Extended tubes. When the inlet or outlet pipe runs on into the chamber, the ring of space behind it is a closed quarter-wave pocket of area S₂ − S₁ at the tube’s mouth, a shunt −j (ρc ÷ (S₂ − S₁)) cot kl (Munjal, Acoustics of Ducts and Mufflers, 1987, 2.13–2.14 and 3.7, stationary medium; with mean flow his eq. 3.97 adds the loss K of Table 3.1, left out here as the chamber is lossless). The open chamber between the mouths is a plain duct and the three are multiplied as transfer matrices. Munjal’s double-tuned chamber, inlet at half and outlet at a quarter of the chamber length, tunes out the first two troughs; the Mufflers tab sets those with one button and reports each pocket’s quarter-wave note.
    • 
      
  • Resonator placement. Side resonators attenuate most at or near the pressure antinodes of the mode they target and least at the nodes (SAE 940614). The page places antinodes every half wavelength from the closed end (valve or turbine), using the same closed-open pipe as the drone check.
    • 
      
  • Muffler types. Packed straight-through designs are generally the loudest and least restrictive (CJ Pony Parts), turbo mufflers generally the quietest, and chambered ones in between (The Drive). In the parts list, a sound level marked “maker’s words” is the maker’s own rating or description. Where the maker gives none, the level is estimated from the type using that order, and is marked so. The measured Yoshimura RS-3 figures and the 20% perforated core come from Potente (Acoustics 2005); the shell-thickness and valve figures come from Faurecia’s engineers (Bönnen et al., Automotive NVH Technology, 2016).
    • 
      
  • Parts tab. Mufflers, resonators, flex pipes, mandrel bends, merge collectors and crossovers by brand and model, including Flowmaster, Borla, MagnaFlow, Vibrant, Black Widow, Spintech, Stainless Bros, Ticon, JMD Tubes and Formula Z. A part a maker does not publish dimensions for is left out rather than guessed; add it as a custom part with your own measurements. In Fusion, the build list is placed along an auto-routed pipe: each part slides along the route and turns about its axis until its case clears the scan by the most, and the pipe is then routed into and out of it. Where a maker says an inlet is offset but not by how much, the offset is taken as close to the case edge as the pipe allows and flagged so you can measure it.
    • 
      
  • Auto-routing through a scan. In Fusion, the scan (a mesh body) and any solids are the space limits. The router finds a way through on a grid, then fits a polyline whose corners are rounded to your bend radius, keeping your gap from the scan and between tubes, the straight you need at each end and between bends, and the target length when there is one (header primaries come out within a hundredth of a millimeter of each other in testing). The finished centerline is then checked against the scan’s actual triangles all along its length, so the gap shown is proven, not estimated. The tube is a sketch plus a pipe feature sized by user parameters, so it stays editable. A route that needs bends tighter than one tube diameter, or more bending than a bender can clamp, is flagged with the way to build it: welded mandrel sections, pie cuts, or a short metal-printed section (Protolabs DMLS design guide; ESAB on 304 to 316 filler).
    • 
      
  • Norbye, The Wankel Engine (1971). Read for the rotary port-timing card on the Headers tab: the Curtiss-Wright RC2-60 U10 and U5 port events (pp. 244, 456) converted from eccentric-shaft to crank-equivalent degrees by 2/3, Jones’s 20% peak-power gain and back-pressure sensitivity of peripheral intake ports (p. 210), NSU’s 30% at 6,000 rpm and its best 50° intake closing on the KKM-502 (pp. 124 to 125), the geometric rule that side ports cannot overlap (p. 263), the Ro-80’s separate silencer train per rotor (p. 146), the reactor-core temperatures of 1,700 to 1,900 °F (p. 344) and NSU’s 36% exhaust heat share (p. 121). Rejected: Daimler-Benz’s “volumetric efficiency 110 to 115% at 2,000 rpm” (p. 264), which can only be a delivery ratio with short-circuited charge or a misprint, and Norbye’s “4 to 5° of advance corresponds to 27 to 30° in a piston engine”, which uses an unexplained factor of six. The book has no exhaust-system design content; it is a journalist’s history that lifts its numbers from SAE papers, cited as such. This book, Smith and Wenner and Vizard had been thought image-only scans; read locally all three carried a usable text layer, so the figures were read from page images and the text from the layer.
    • 
      
  • Smith and Wenner, The Design and Tuning of Competition Engines, 6th ed. (1977). Taken: the Tri-Y “good average” lengths of 18 in to the first junction and 24 in on to the second (Fig. 9-18), now beside the Headers tab’s Tri-Y result; the Jaguar XK trumpet family (Fig. 8-27: 32.5, 21.5, 15, 8 in and none, peaking at 3,300 to 5,000 rpm) as validation points on the Intake tab; the port-velocity limits of about 160 ft/s intake and 240 ft/s exhaust and the 2 to 3 psi average back pressure of a good system (pp. 37 to 38); the cam-timing presets by specific output (Fig. 3-5); the advice that a diameter step well downstream of the port helps and one right after it hurts (p. 310); and the 7 to 8 psi stock-engine boost rule (p. 376). Shown but not used for design: the one pipe formula, P = A·S·D² ÷ (1400·d²), which has no rpm term and lands about 50% longer than Bell or Vizard; it sits on the 4-Stroke and Headers tabs labelled as a 1950s upper bound. Most of the book’s quantitative exhaust content is deferred to Smith and Morrison, already read.
    • 
      
  • Vizard, How to Modify Ford S.O.H.C. Engines (1983), chapters 2, 3, 11 and 14, and the chapter 5 figures. Fig. 5-8, previously unreadable, gives primary length against peak rpm (33.5 in at 5,500 to 28 in at 7,250 from the dyno, 26 to 22 in to 9,500 extrapolated) with stepped primary IDs of 1¾ to 2 in; it is shown beside this page’s Bell-formula length with the dyno and extrapolated points marked, and the Esslinger A/B test behind the oversize stepped primary (+8 to 10 hp, Fig. 5-3) in the caption. From chapter 2 the horsepower-from-airflow rule, 1.05 × cfm per port at 25 in H₂O on a four, restated as 0.248 bhp per cfm per cylinder at 28 in, valid only with exhaust flow 70 to 75% of intake, which also resolves an earlier OCR reading of “10%” for that ratio. From chapter 11 the TO4B V-1 map and the surge example, the trim and A/R rules, and the boost-CR-octane chart (Fig. 11-3) as a table marked 1983 and estimated. Two corrections to earlier batches: the back-pressure loss on the 2 L at 3.5 psi reads 6.7 bhp on the page image, not the 6.1 the text layer gave; and his text and Fig. 11-3 disagree by one octane grade (10 psi at 8.3:1 on 95 octane in the text, 100 octane on the chart), noted on the table. His own 219 bhp engine wanting 21 to 22 in primaries against the chart’s 28 in at 7,200 rpm is also noted. Nitrous as anti-lag (0.02 lb/s per psi) was not added, since the page has no nitrous input.
    • 
      
  • Rohrauer, “Induction and Exhaust” lecture deck (R2 2025). Every slide was read as an image this time. It reproduces Kirkpatrick and Ferguson, Heywood, Stone and Taylor, so those are cited rather than the deck: Taylor’s valve fractions (0.44/0.38 two-valve, 0.33/0.29 four-valve) and Mach index Z ≤ 0.6 with VE ≈ 0.75/Z at choked flow, the flow-coefficient table against lift ratio, Stone’s charge-density and intercooler-effectiveness formulas and chart points, Stone’s best-IVC family read as 3° ABDC per m/s of mean piston speed (this page’s reading), Heywood’s single-runner VE curves (780, 680, 520 mm), Stone’s 4-2-1 lengths of 500 and 700 mm, and the Garrett A/R comparison. Rejected: its wave-reflection slide, whose string-wave animations say a free end reflects upright and a fixed end inverted, which is backwards for gas pressure waves (a closed valve returns a compression as a compression, an open end inverts it; Blair, Heywood and Davies agree, and this page’s wave simulation already does it the gas way), and its “critical pressure ratio of about 3” for exhaust, which lower γ moves toward 1.8, not 3 (1.86 at γ 1.35); the cylinder-to-port ratio at opening is often above 3, which is a different statement. An earlier note that its tables were scrambled is superseded: the figure carries Taylor’s fractions as given above.
    • 
      
  • Mathematical and Computer Modelling 57 (2013), the engine papers. The zip held the whole issue; four papers beyond Antebas et al. are engine-relevant. Olmeda, Dolz, Arnau and Reyes-Belmonte (pp. 1847 to 1852) measured heat into the turbine case at up to 45% of the exhaust energy at low speed and load, now a note in the Intake tab’s turbo section as the reason manifolds get wrapped. Macian, Torregrosa, Broatch, Niven and Amphlett (pp. 1867 to 1875) show a linear source model of exhaust noise holds for about the first four or five engine orders and goes erratic above, so the Sound tab’s tailpipe tones are trustworthy at the firing fundamental and its low harmonics only. Serrano et al. (pp. 1751 to 1759) and Galindo et al. (pp. 1957 to 1964) are numerical-method papers; the one point kept is that a long tailpipe with wall friction reflects weakly even when open, so an ideal anechoic end under-predicts back-reflection. The other 55 papers are off-topic and were not read.
    • 
      
  • Shop videos. These were watched with an AI video model. Figures read off on-screen dynos are shop tests on one car each, not controlled studies, and they are used here only as checks. On a Huracán, a 14 in straight test pipe after the collector made 486 hp against 469 hp as delivered, the shop’s valved X-pipe system 483 hp and the incoming 2.5 in system 472 hp (Fluid MotorUnion, Huracán). That fits the idea used here that a short open pipe is the ceiling and a full system only loses less. A 2.25 to 2.5 in pipe swap on a 245 hp Corvette lost power from 2,800 to 4,400 RPM until timing was advanced 2° (C4 Corvette). An LS3 Camaro gained 32 hp at the wheels with stepped primaries, an X-pipe and megaphones in place of a necked-down single 3 in pipe (LS3 Camaro). Their megaphone, 14 in long from 2.5 to 4 in, is a 6.1° included angle, inside Jennings’ 8° (FMU masterclass). The 21° they quote for a merge is the standard convergent angle of a classical Venturi flow meter (ISO 5167-4; fluid mechanics text), and 0.61 is the contraction coefficient of a sharp-edged orifice. Applying either to an X-pipe is their judgment, not a measurement. Stepped primaries partly reflect each pulse at every step, which is why F1 headers were stepped (Maisteer, F1 sound). The 1-D model here handles steps. The firing-order arithmetic in the Lexus LFA video matches the Sound tab: 5th order at 6,000 RPM is 500 Hz, and a cross-plane V8’s 4th order at 3,427 RPM is 228 Hz (LFA exhaust). On a V6, each bank of three gets a pulse every 240°, the reason true duals sound raspy (V6 Charger, Bronco 2.7, GLE 400). One claim is not used: one video gives the speed of sound in exhaust as 319 m/s cold and 841 m/s at 850 °C. The physics, a = √(γRT), gives about 340 m/s in cold air and about 650 m/s at 850 °C, and the calculator uses that formula. Six more shop videos were added later: an EcoBoost Raptor built with two megaphones into one 4 in centre section and the biggest muffler that fits, to tame V6 rasp (FMU, Raptor); a turbo Jeep whose wastegate tee was moved off a 90° branch onto a 45° so the gas feeds it, with the shop’s rule that a wastegate sits as close to the turbo as possible and on the outside of a bend (turbo Jeep); a twin-turbo Trans Am where a 4.5 in centre pipe had to split into two 3.5 in pipes to clear the axle and tank, and a valve on one side took care of drone (Trans Am); a Mercedes S65 where the shop quotes a rule of 1 in of pipe diameter per 100 hp and tunes megaphone position by ear, warning that a megaphone or chamber near the tail end can drone unless the pipe steps back down (S65); a V12 with 2¼ in primaries into 4-1 collectors with 3½ in outlets (V12); and a supercharged E55 whose restricted filters capped the dyno at 428 hp against 483 hp with no filters, cured with a 3.5 in aluminum intake and canister filters, the remaining 18 hp put down to heat soak (E55). The 1 in per 100 hp rule is a shop figure with no test behind it; the Intake tab sizes tubes by air speed instead, and the Headers tab by displacement and RPM. The E55 video’s on-screen intake formula came through the transcript garbled and was not used; its message, that a choked filter shows as a hard power cut on the dyno, is covered by the K&N filter-capacity check. A seventh video explains intake runner length with a syringe: a long runner lets the moving air column pack the cylinder before the valve shuts (a ram effect), a short one does not, and resonance is a second-order effect on top of that; it argues for tuning the Helmholtz peak to minimise losses across the band rather than chase one peak (runner length explained). That matches Engelman, who found the plain Helmholtz peak broad, and the wave simulation here ranks designs by average torque for the same reason. Three more came through as transcripts only (the video quota ran out): The Fabrication Series dynoed every bend type on a ~145 whp car with a 2 in system and found mandrel, crush, crinkle and pie-cut bends within a few horsepower of each other (mandrel 144.8, crush 145.8, pie cuts 146.3, no bends about 146 to 148, no exhaust 149) with back pressure about 1.4 to 1.5 psi; the one loser was a system of nothing but bends, 15% longer with 176% more bends, at 3 to 4 psi. Their rule for crush bends is to go up one pipe size; stainless against aluminised steel was about 1 dB (all bends to no bends). (A hobby ebook in the reading list claimed a mandrel bend flows 35% more than a crimp bend with no source; it was never used here, and this test is why.) Vizard’s long “zero power loss street legal exhaust” lecture (PowerTech 10) repeats the short version’s numbers (2.3 cfm per open-exhaust horsepower, the 8 × one-cylinder termination box, the 704 hp Corvette) and adds his explanation of the back-pressure myth: a straight-through glasspack keeps the flow but moves the tuned length to the wrong value, which magazine tests then read as “needs back pressure”. Four more, read from their captions (the video frames could not be downloaded): an explainer on stepped primaries (Speed Mediums) says the step makes a second reflection that keeps the waves working above the RPM the length suits, and puts it halfway along the primary, as the 50/50 stepped profile here does (his reasoning, no test); a dyno test on a 1600 cc Toyota 4A (Stepped Headers, dyno tested) found a small gain from the smaller section out of the head, a step about 140 mm from the head or a cone, over the same tube all the way, the step and the cone much the same (one car, the step run on another day, the dyno sheet not readable here); Borla’s Polyphonic Harmonizer (Borla) sets several parallel pipes’ lengths and diameters so their notes stand in consonant intervals such as a perfect fifth, the way organ pipes do (no numbers given), and David Borla explains it (GarageInsiderTV) as asymmetric dual exhausts, one note from each side, a perfect fifth apart like a guitar power chord, sometimes with a third note: the Sound tab’s “Two notes on true duals” gives the lengths for that; and a truck build that cured a 117 Hz drone (a V8 at 1,750 RPM, dual 3 in into a single 4 in) with a 2.5 in J-pipe 28⅞ in long (quarter-wave resonator build): the drone was almost gone at 1,800, a little left at 1,500 (about 95 Hz), and quietest at 2,000 to 2,100, which puts the branch gas near 150 °C rather than ambient; the Mufflers tab now gives a start length for a hot branch. The same shop repeated the bend test on a turbo Subaru (about 375 whp, open 2.5 in system, no cat, about 130 dB), read from its captions and on-screen dyno (every exhaust bend on a turbo car): mandrel 376.6 hp and 325 lb-ft at about 1.5 psi; 2.5 in crush bends 380.7 hp and 3 in crush bends 379 hp; pie cuts 369.7 hp; crinkle bends 367.7 hp with the gauge reaching about 3 psi; single miters 359.2 hp at about 3 psi; a 21-bend system about 20% longer 346 hp at about 3.5 psi; 2 in square tubing with miters, about the inside area of 2.5 in round, 326.8 hp with the 4 psi gauge pinned; and eight loops, more than twice the length, 365.3 hp. So with more flow the bend-type losses grow from noise to 7 to 17 hp, and a sharp turn costs most; mandrel and crush bends stay level. The loops gave what they heard as two notes side by side up to near the top of the pull; a pipe more than twice as long has its own resonances, at n·c ÷ 2L, about half as far apart, so more of them sit among the firing harmonics, and the wave model and the Sound tab’s estimate carry pipe length. Their spectrum overlay put mild steel slightly lower in pitch and level than stainless; at these levels one pull to the next differs as much, and the calculator gives the wall material no tone of its own (their earlier quieter test measured about 1 dB). Their back-pressure gauge readings are low for this flow (about 0.37 kg/s through 2.5 in tube is near 3 psi of velocity head alone), so they are used only as an order. A Ford V10 build with its own four-valve heads (Build It Yourself, Tuned In podcast) explains its F1 sound the way the Sound tab works it out: equal-length primaries so the pulses reach each collector evenly, the banks firing alternately, and the banks brought together (as an X-pipe does on a V8) so the pulses that meet double the pitch; they modelled the rest of the system on the Lexus LFA’s. On an even-fire V10 each bank alone takes a pulse every 144°, the 2.5th order, and joined the 5th: 500 Hz at 6,000 RPM. More checks, read from on-screen dyno sheets and captions on the owner’s computer. The same 4A-GE shop put a restriction in the exhaust and logged the pressure (exhaust back pressure, dyno tested): at 0.4, 0.9 and 2.4 psi at the top the curves lie together (about 130 kW at the wheels near 8,000 RPM); at 7.5 psi peak power fell about 5%, and at 18 psi by more than 15% with the curve breaking up. That fits the rule here that a free pipe is the ceiling and a few psi costs little on this engine. Its megaphone test (exhaust megaphone angle, dyno tested) ran 5°, 6° and 9° megaphones (the video does not say whether that is the wall or the included angle), a straight 3 in pipe and the full exhaust: the top end is the same within the lines, the 5° gave the smoothest curve from 3,000 to 5,500 RPM, and the 9° fell away first above 9,500; Jennings’s 8° included angle used here sits in that range. An explainer (337 Speed, Explained ep. 27) uses the same primary-area rule as the Headers tab (RPM × cylinder cubic inches ÷ 88,200: 2.07 in², 1.62 in inside, 1¾ in tube for a 6,000 RPM K20) and quotes 35 to 38 in primaries for street engines and 28 to 30 in for racing ones as rules of thumb; the Headers tab works the length out from the tuning RPM and cam instead. A history of the exhaust (New Mind) gives NACA Report 1192’s three sources (blowdown pulse, flow noise, shell noise), most energy below 500 Hz on the firing order (a four at 3,000 RPM: 100 Hz), 500 to 650 m/s for sound in exhaust gas, extended tubes of half and a quarter of the chamber, a quarter-wave stub working at odd multiples, and 0 to 2°, 7 to 9° cones for a two-stroke header and diffuser; all agree with what the calculator uses. A two-stroke racer (2Stroke Stuffing, stingers) starts a stinger at about 3.1 × √hp in mm (he credits Fritz Overmars) and needed 13 to 14 mm at Bonneville against 17 mm at home, since power and outside pressure both drop at altitude; the Two-Stroke tab sizes the stinger from the header (0.58 to 0.62 of it, Jennings), which does not follow altitude; his result says to go smaller there. Maisteer’s V12 (fixing the worst sounding V12) found titanium, stainless and mild steel headers of the same shape close in sound, the shape mattering far more; a 12-into-1 with a large step into the collector sounded worse than two 6-into-1s with shallow merges; and the worst sound of all turned out to be one bank not firing, so check that every cylinder fires before tuning the pipe. A turbo LS build flowing the heads backwards (Nivlac57, reverse-flow LT) clocks its eight primaries round the 8-into-1 collector in firing order; the Headers tab now lists that order for each collector. Sound-only clips, with no numbers: an 8-into-1 on a 347 Ford (Track Day Classics) and 8-into-1 and 6-into-1 headers on an E30, a 280Z, a Ferrari 599 and a Stratos (compilation).

  • Port shape and cam card. A port that is not round is given the diameter of a round port with the same area: an oval as an ellipse, a racetrack as a rectangle with half-circle ends (whichever way width and height are entered), and a rectangle with corner radius r as width × height − (4 − π)r². The cam card figures are the usual arithmetic: duration = opening + 180 + closing, overlap = intake opening + exhaust closing, centerlines (closing − opening + 180) ÷ 2, lobe separation their mean.
    • 
      
  • Helmholtz intake tuning. From H. W. Engelman, Design of a Tuned Intake Manifold, ASME paper 73-WA/DGP-2 (1973): the cylinder at mid-stroke, volume = half the swept volume × (CR + 1) ÷ (CR − 1), and its runner resonate together, and the runner helps most where that resonance is about 2.1 times the crank speed. Runner area is sized for the 200 ft/s mean speed the paper found best. With a plenum and the tube feeding it, the paper’s two-resonator model is solved exactly in place of its charts. On the paper’s own worked example this gives 3,415 RPM where the paper gives 3,400, and 4,535 RPM for the upper peak where the paper reads 4,540 off its chart.
    • 
      
  • Engine Simulator file. The 4-Stroke tab writes an engine file for Engine Simulator (Community Edition v0.1.14a or the open-source engine-sim) for a rough listen. Bore, stroke, compression, cam, header and intake sizes come from the tab. Head flow, masses, ignition and gearing come from an Engine Simulator example engine, using the values in the MIT-licensed open-source repository, each named in the file with its line. Files for 18 engines, from a single to a V12, were compiled with Engine Simulator’s own script compiler, and every cylinder’s firing point, compression and valve events were read back within 0.1°. Two of them were then run in Engine Simulator v0.1.14a itself: both started, idled and took a full dyno pull. The pull also showed that ideal-orifice flow coefficients for the real pipe sizes over-read power by about 75% (913 hp for a mild 350), so the export now uses the example engine’s flow ratings (521 hp for the same file, still high; a 2.0 L four read 151 hp). Engine Simulator treats each exhaust as one volume with the pipe length as a sound delay, and the muffler sound comes from a recorded file, so it cannot judge a header. The wave simulation does that. A third target, Arcindweld fork with the 1-D exhaust, writes the same file plus the pipe geometry the fork understands (primary diameter, collector diameter and length, megaphone length and exit, tailpipe, cell size), which switches its one-dimensional exhaust model on for that file while the shipped engines keep the original behaviour. In the fork each exhaust system is a network of 1-D pipes (one primary per cylinder, a constant-pressure junction, collector, cone and tailpipe, characteristic open end) solved with a MUSCL-Hancock/HLLC scheme ported from this page’s wave simulation, and the sound is taken at the tailpipe exit, so header length changes both the torque curve and the harmonics. Its validation: Sod’s shock tube within 0.34% of the exact solution (density, 400 cells), a closed-open pulse returns at −0.66% of 2L/c, quarter-wave resonance within 0.15%, a temperature front crosses its junctions without a pressure step, mass and energy conserved to round-off, all 25 shipped engines run, legacy mode bit-identical. Each cylinder’s exhaust port feeds its primary through a characteristic (valve-type) boundary solved at every one of Engine Simulator’s fluid sub-steps, and the pipes advance at their own CFL step, so the torque converges: the test four at 6,000 RPM makes 141, 138, 137 and 137 N·m on 4, 2, 1 and 0.5 cm cells and 140, 138 and 139 N·m at 15, 20 and 40 kHz, against a spread of about 3 N·m between runs with different seeds of Engine Simulator’s random burn, and 4 cm and 2 cm cells agree on every primary-length change from 4,000 to 7,000 RPM and within 5% from 4,000 to 7,800 RPM. Known limits, stated in its docs: the 4-1 low-RPM hole is real but exaggerated (no junction losses, lumped intake, fixed wall temperature), the default 4 cm cells cost about three times the legacy model’s time on a V8 or a flat four, and Engine Simulator needs a simulation step of no more than about 2° of crank (the fork export sets the frequency to three times the redline for that). Treat its torque as a ranking between headers, not a dyno number.

  • Header Wizard comparison. All five Fast Header Wizard v4.8 Pro programs (singles and twins; fours; fives and tens; threes, sixes and twelves; V8s) were run. For a 2.0 L four (84 × 89 mm, 11.5:1, 160 kW at 7,800 RPM, cam 32/44/48/20, 4-2-1, 43 × 31 mm racetrack port 150 mm long), its port size (37.88 mm), cam figures (256° and 248°, 52° overlap, 100° lobe separation, 4° advanced) and mean effective pressure (12.47 bar) match this calculator’s. Its runners came out 1.4 to 1.7 times the length the primary-length formula here gives, in every program: 893 mm against 554 mm from the valve to the last merge on that four, 1,238 against 865 mm on a 350 V8, 887 against 633 mm on a five and 781 against 469 mm on a 450 single. It does not publish its method, so neither can be called right from its output. Things to know when using it: entering a racetrack port with width and height the other way round silently gives a smaller port (34.53 mm here) and lengthened every section about 17%; its rectangle-with-corner-radius option gave 42.51 mm for a 38 × 35 mm port with 6 mm corners, larger than the 41.15 mm of the same rectangle with square corners, so that option adds area where it should subtract it; the port boxes drop decimal points; the turbo setting and the application choice changed nothing in any run; its termination box is always 8 times one cylinder’s displacement (which is David Vizard’s published termination-box rule, so that part has a traceable source), and its intake plenum about 1.36 times the displacement it feeds, neither with a stated source. Its 2nd-harmonic intake length follows ECD ÷ RPM like Grape Ape Racing’s formula, with a different constant. Its single-cylinder Megabomb output (chamber size, cone lengths and hole pattern) and its 6-2-1 layout are covered here by the resonance chamber on the 4-Stroke tab and the two-stage merge on the Headers tab.

Its mean effective pressure (11.85 bar) matches this calculator’s. Its tuned length to the stinger was 868.5 mm, 1.4% longer than Blair’s 856 mm at 650 °C (it implies 677 °C), with section shares close to Blair’s (header 8%, diffusers 55%, belly 12%, baffle 25%); its belly was 108.1 mm (2.84 port diameters, Blair’s Grand Prix constant gives 3.25) and its stinger 20.4 mm (0.54, Blair 0.60), 163 mm long against Blair’s stinger as long as the baffle. Its powerband slider changed only the first two diffuser diameters (65.1 and 78.2 mm at the race end, 54.0 and 71.1 mm at 150). Its straight-header version came out 0.7% longer in every section than the curved one. Dual Power adds a second tuned length with an inner cone in the baffle, half perforated, ending in a small inner pipe: on this 125 its second length was 975.7 mm (12.3% longer, about 10,240 RPM), the cone 271.9 mm from the belly end (1.26 baffle lengths), the pipe 50.7 mm long at 11.9 mm; on a 250 (66.4 × 72 mm, 50 hp at 8,500 RPM, 190°, 42 mm port 70 mm long) 1,237.3 mm (12.6% longer), 345.4 mm (1.27), 65.5 mm at 13.6 mm, the pipe ending at the second length both times. It does not publish its method; the 2-Stroke tab’s dual power insert follows those proportions, with the cone’s mouth made the widest that fits inside the baffle. Its sample engine, a vintage Maico 490 (86.5 × 83 mm, 53 hp at 6,500 RPM, 179° exhaust, 123° transfers, 43 mm port 55 mm long, 7.48 bar), came out 1,189 mm to the stinger with a 89.3 mm belly and a 22.8 mm stinger; Blair’s method here gives 1,257 mm (474 °C gas on the line toward his road engine), a 96.8 mm belly and a 30.1 mm stinger. Across its three runs its gas temperature rises faster with BMEP than Blair’s (about 395 °C at 7.5 bar, 593 °C at 10.6, 677 °C at 11.9). The 2-Stroke tab’s “From the engine” design does the same job with Blair’s published method throughout: BMEP from the power, gas temperature and diameter constants from BMEP, two or three diffuser cones, the blowdown angle, and a powerband setting.

  • Making the intake by 3D printing. The How it will be made selector adds FDM on the shop’s Bambu X1 Carbon, SLS or MJF nylon from a service, and laser-sintered AlSi10Mg. Every material row is a maker datasheet (Bambu, Polymaker, HP via Weerg, EOS, CRP), HDT per ISO 75 on annealed, dry specimens; the suggested continuous temperatures and boost limits are the research notes’ own derating (the lower of HDT₁.₈ − 30 °C or 0.85 × HDT₀.₄₅, Tg − 20 °C for PC and ASA, and the vendor service cases), and are labelled as such. Design temperatures come from measured values: 201 °C in a charge pipe after the compressor (MotoIQ), 44 to 107 °C on a diesel manifold wall (CRP), 55 to 90 °C on printed flanges (Audizine), a 0 to 100 °C OE test envelope (PRI). The wall solver is thin-wall hoop stress for round sections and simply supported plate bending for flats, against the hot, wet, across-layer strength at a safety factor of 3, because every published failure is a flat panel, a boss or a flange and never a round wall; the temperature factor (1 at 23 °C to 0.4 at the 1.8 MPa HDT) is an assumption, since no vendor publishes hot strength. Where sheets disagree the lower figure is used: Bambu PC lists 117 °C at 1.8 MPa and 112 at 0.45; Bambu PPS-CF claims 235 °C at 1.8 MPa where Polymaker’s PPS-CF10 claims 133; PA12 is 95 °C (HP), 86 (EOS) or “147” (JLC3DP, load unstated); a third-party ISO 75 test on unannealed PPA-CF prints gave 82.5 to 83 °C for two brands against Bambu’s 196 on annealed specimens; HP’s 3 bar race manifold does not say gauge or absolute. Across-layer strengths for the EOS and Windform powders are not published and take PA2200’s ratio. Data Driven Performance (datadrivenperf.com), often cited as a printed-intake maker, sells one product: an FDM cold-air tube for the 2009–15 CTS-V (6 in filter tapering to a 4.5 in MAF housing, port-matched to a 103, 112 or 120 mm throttle, with a heat enclosure), one piece over 350 mm long with visible layer lines and an embossed logo, polymer unstated. Its “test proven” and “highest flowing” claims have no published numbers, methodology or reviews, and the only Gen 2 CTS-V intake dyno figures found are a competitor’s (stock 457 whp, Airaid 478). Such a tube works for ordinary reasons: a 6 in filter cuts face velocity to 44% of a 4 in inlet, a steady taper gives the MAF a flat profile, the port match removes a step, and the enclosure keeps the air cooler before the blower multiplies every degree; the gain is bounded by the few kPa of pre-compressor depression, single digits of percent in density. It is not a manifold and says nothing about runners or plenums. The bellmouth proportions are Blair and Cahoon’s (Race Engine Technology, September 2006) via a forum reproduction; the discharge coefficients offered beside them are from memory of the paper and marked to verify. Insert pull-out is Sculpteo’s MJF PA12 test; prices are JLC3DP’s and 3D People’s published rates, and the metal range is a placeholder from bureau marketing and a forum thread.

  • Charge pipes. The hot and cold sides are routed like any other tube, with the intercooler, turbo and exhaust as keep-outs. Blow-off valves and sensor bungs from the Parts tab are weld-on fittings: the router stands each one on a straight run, clocked in 45° steps for the most room, the valve nearest the throttle (Turbosmart and GFB) and never on the inside of a bend, and proves its gap against the scan’s triangles like a tube. The bead, coupler, clamp, valve and sensor rules in the charge pipe section are each tied to their source; what no maker publishes (bead width, most valve flange sizes, an ovality limit for automotive tube) is left out rather than guessed. Bell’s rules. From Corky Bell, Maximum Boost (Bentley, 1997), read in full: charge-pipe speed against a Mach 0.4 ceiling on about 1.5 cfm per horsepower (pp. 61–62), about 1% of flow per 90° of turning and cones tapering one diameter in four lengths (pp. 62–63), the hose-joint load as pipe area × boost (a 2 in joint at 20 psi carries 63 lb, so tie-bar the pipes), intercooler internal flow area about 6 in² per 100 hp with 45% of the charge face open and thin cores over thick (pp. 54–59, his NSX 375 hp → 23 in² → 15 × 3 in core), a core drop under 2 psi at 1.5 × engine cfm with each psi lost there costing about 2 psi of turbine-inlet pressure (pp. 72–73), and turbine-inlet pressure of 2 to 2.5 × boost as the turbine-size check (pp. 37, 169–170). One builder’s rules, with one measured car behind the last.
