  • Stainless Bros, Ticon Industries and Cone Engineering. 2,136 fabrication parts from these three makers are on the Parts tab, one entry per size and part number: mandrel bends (OD, wall, centreline radius, angle, legs), straight tube, pie cuts (angle per cut, cuts per 90°, radius), slip joints, reducers and transitions, cones and megaphones (Cone Engineering’s taper column is the included angle; where only the two diameters and the length are published the angle is worked out as 2·atan((D₂−D₁)/2L) and marked), merge collectors with the inlet count as a number so they can be filtered by cylinder group (Cone’s 2- to 8-into-1 conical collectors give inlet OD, outlet and length for all 197; the merge angle is only published for the 3D-printed Stainless Bros and Ticon units), V-band flanges and clamps, header, turbo and exhaust flanges (thickness is missing on most Stainless Bros and Ticon flanges and is shown as not published), muffler bodies, perforated cores, end caps and ready-made race mufflers, plus Ticon’s titanium velocity stacks. Ticon’s catalogue came from its store data, Stainless Bros from 807 product pages, Cone Engineering from its PDF price sheets checked against every part number. Material is carried on every entry (304, 321, 316, Inconel 625, CP1 titanium, mild). Gaps are left as “not published”: slip-joint lengths (no maker states them), leg lengths on “with leg” elbows, centreline radius on Alucon aluminium bends, and 36 Stainless Bros option-only pages without part numbers.
    • 
      
  • OpenWAM. The 4-Stroke tab writes a complete OpenWAM 2.2 case (openwam.org, the free 1-D engine code from CMT, Universitat Politècnica de València): one .wam per engine speed with the cylinders on this collector, their valves with lift and discharge curves, intake runners, primaries, collector segments and megaphone as pipes, plus a batch file that runs them in turn and a reader for the AVG.DAT output. The writer is a line-for-line port of a Python generator that was checked against OpenWAM’s shipped single-cylinder example and then on 4-1, Tri-Y, stepped-primary and dual-bank V8 cases that all run to completion with no warnings (a 2.0 L four at 6,000 RPM: 195 N·m net, 107% delivered VE); the JavaScript output matches the Python writer byte for byte on 98 cases. Combustion (Wiebe), heat transfer (Woschni), friction and wall temperatures are generator defaults held constant across runs, so OpenWAM’s absolute torque is not a dyno number; the point is that header changes show up in the same physics the calculator’s own wave model approximates, including the port, the collector and the megaphone. The pipes are cut into 10 mm cells: at 5 mm the net torque moves by under 1% (the four at 4,000 and 6,000 RPM, a dual-bank V8 at 5,500 RPM), but in the outflow’s order spectrum an order that sits in a dip between pipe resonances can move by many dB (up to 15 dB on one test model), so read that spectrum as a pattern, not order by order. OpenWAM’s mean flows inside the pipes are no mass balance either (its valve and open-end boundaries do not conserve mass); the cylinders’ own masses, which the reader uses for torque and VE, are consistent. Side-branch chambers (a resonator can on a primary) are written as a junction, a neck and a closed volume on every primary, with the neck’s flow area and length the wave simulation uses (a neck shorter than three cells is lengthened with its area raised by the same factor, which keeps its Helmholtz tuning). The WAMer front end was not used; the files are written directly.
    • 
      
  • OpenWAM for two-strokes. The 2-Stroke tab (From the engine) writes the designed chamber into a two-stroke OpenWAM case: the piston uncovering the exhaust and transfer windows (their exposed area worked out from the window shape and the crank-slider law), the crankcase as a volume the piston drives, a reed valve (petals as a lumped mass and spring from their size and material) or a piston-controlled intake port, Wiebe combustion, and the chamber as conical pipes. OpenWAM 2.2 closes a two-stroke cycle at the latest intake-side port, which would be transfer closing; a dummy port that never flows makes it exhaust closing, so the chamber’s plugging pulse counts. It has no loop-scavenging model (the cylinder is perfectly mixed), so trapping and power read low; brake power adds the crankcase pumping work from the INS file and takes off a friction estimate. The writer is a port of a Python generator, the same bytes on 52 test specs; on a 125 MX it gave 31 hp at 12,000 RPM against 14 hp for a straight pipe of the same length.
    • 
      
  • Intake CFD (OpenFOAM). The Intake tab writes a complete OpenFOAM v2412 case (openfoam.com, ESI’s free release) for the tube on the tab: a body-fitted axisymmetric mesh (blockMesh, wall-resolved at y+ ≈ 1) of the mouth, an atmosphere region in front of it so the entry flow is computed rather than imposed, the tube, the cone to the throttle and an outlet extension; steady compressible RANS (rhoSimpleFoam, perfect gas, Sutherland viscosity) with Menter’s k-ω SST turbulence model, the engine’s cycle-mean airflow at the peak-power RPM set at the outlet, and a report script that gives PR, K, Cd, Blair and Lau’s vena-contracta CD for 1-D models and the MAF-plane uniformity. Checked against Blair and Cahoon’s FLUENT and QUB flow-bench study of 23 mm bellmouths (Race Engine Technology, Sept. 2006): at the published pressure ratios the sharp-edged pipe flows 30.34 g/s against their 30.02 (+1.1%), the 6 mm radius 36.30 against 34.83 (+4.2%) and the elliptical bellmouth 38.06 against 36.15 (+5.3%). The ranking is right, and so is the pattern: the radius gains a lot over the plain end and the bellmouth only a little more (+23% and +2.3% at PR 1.039, against Blair’s “near constant 16%” and “a mere 1.5%”), the first gain larger than theirs. The 4 to 5% on the rounded inlets is the size of the dependence on where the static-pressure station sits, about 1 to 1.2% per pipe diameter, which the article does not specify. Mesh refinement from medium to fine moves the airflow by 0.15% or less. What it does not do: the flow is steady, so there is no pulsation, no wave tuning and no sound (those are the wave simulation and OpenWAM sections); losses at cycle-mean flow understate the pulse peak (use the flow factor); walls are smooth and adiabatic; the filter element, throttle plate and sensor body are not in the model. The browser writer is a port of the Python generator and matches it byte for byte on 8 axisymmetric cases; tubes with bends are three-dimensional and the download then holds the design and the Python generator for snappyHexMesh.
    • 
      
  • Exhaust component CFD (OpenFOAM). The Headers tab writes the same kind of case for one exhaust part from a CAD STL whose inlet and outlet faces are named: a merge collector, a Tri-Y secondary, an X- or H-pipe section, a muffler or resonator shell or a tailpipe tip. Each inlet is extruded two diameters upstream and fed the engine’s cycle-mean exhaust flow (air × (1 + 1/AFR) at the tuning RPM and VE, split equally between the primaries unless set) as hot gas, 650 °C by default at a header and 400 °C downstream, with air’s gas constant and Sutherland viscosity at that temperature (exhaust gas has a few percent more heat capacity; K is a ratio of pressures, so it hardly notices); the outlet is extruded two diameters and held at ambient static pressure. It reports the total-pressure loss from the inlet faces to the exit face in Pa, kPa and mbar, K in dynamic heads of the inlet gas speed, K to ambient (the exit’s dynamic head included), the back pressure, the flow split between the inlets and the exit velocity uniformity. Checked against known answers: a sudden expansion from 50 to 100 mm bore gives K 0.635 after the friction of its own straight pipes (0.037) is taken off, against Borda–Carnot’s (1 − A₁/A₂)² = 0.562 (0.56 to 0.61 with Idelchik’s correction for the inlet velocity profile); a 90° mandrel bend of 50 mm bore at R/D 1.5 gives K 0.20 for the bend itself (friction of the straights, 0.25, taken off), at the bottom of the 0.20 to 0.30 of Idelchik’s diagrams and Crane TP-410’s 14 fT = 0.27 (medium mesh, gas at 650 °C, inlet 100 m/s, Re about 50,000; both runs converged). So the expansion reads a little high and the bend at the low end of the published range. What it does not do, plainly: the flow is steady, so there is no pulsation, no scavenging or wave tuning between primaries (that is the OpenWAM section), no sound and no heat loss through the walls; a cycle-mean run understates the loss at the pulse peak, which goes with the square of the instantaneous flow. Use it to rank collector shapes, merge angles, crossover sections and tips by their steady loss, not to predict torque.

  • Unequal-length primaries. The Headers tab’s Primary lengths selector takes one length per cylinder (and per Y pair on a Tri-Y, with the pairs typed as built, for example a Subaru 4-2-1 as 1,3 | 2,4). For each primary it shows the RPM this page’s length rule gives for that length (L = 850 × (180 + EVO) ÷ RPM − 3 in, solved for RPM), the wave round trip 2L ÷ a with a = 20.05 √T, and the spread of those times; and for each collector the order content of the pulse-arrival train (firing angle plus L ÷ a, identical pulses), which shows the half orders (0.5, 1.5, 2.5 × crank) that unequal arrival puts into the sound and that equal lengths on an evenly firing collector remove. It is first-order acoustics: the gas velocity, pulse strength and the rest of the system are left out, and Blair’s fuller treatment (Design and Simulation of Four-Stroke Engines, SAE, 1999) was not available to check against. The lengths go into the OpenWAM case (every cylinder with its own primary, the Tri-Y secondaries per pair, open at the collector exit, plus the open-end flow for an order-spectrum reader that splits the simulated outflow into orders), the Engine Simulator file (one primary length per cylinder) and the Fusion route (one target length per port marker). Subaru’s reasons for unequal and equal manifolds are from its engineers in TOYOTA TIMES (2024); no controlled equal-against-unequal dyno or sound test was found.

  • Throttle bodies. 109 bodies are on the Parts tab: Nick Williams (92 to 120 mm, LS, LT, Hellcat), Holley and Sniper (92 to 105 mm and the 4150/4500 units with their cfm), BBK, Ford Performance and Ford OEM (the Coyote’s 80 mm and the GT350’s 87 mm are single bores; only Cobra Jet and GT500 are twins), FAST, Edelbrock, Accufab, Wilson, GM, Mopar and Honda OEM sizes with part numbers, Bosch’s 0 280 750 drive-by-wire series from 32 to 82 mm with the standalone-ECU kits that use them, and ITBs from Jenvey, Borla, AT Power and Heritage with Kinsler’s throttle sizes. The airflow basis is displacement × RPM ÷ 3,456 at the VE entered (Holley, Candela). Carburettor-style cfm ratings are taken at 1.5 inHg for four-barrels and 3 inHg for two-barrels (divide by 1.414 to compare); the claim that 4500-flange units are rated at 3 inHg could not be confirmed and is not used. The dyno tests behind the “bigger rarely helps” note are listed with their sources in the Intake section; makers’ horsepower claims for throttle bodies are quoted on the cards as claims.   • MAF sensors. 105 sensors and housings are on the Parts tab under MAF housings: GM (LS1 3-wire 85 mm, the 5-wire tube, LS3/LS7/LS9/LSA card 15865791 and its replacements, the 2009-15 truck card, Gen V LT 8-pin cards, Duramax), Ford (Fox 5.0 through the 2024 Coyote, Cobra and Lightning 90 mm class, GT500, EcoBoost, Power Stroke), Mopar (Hemi, Hellcat, Viper, Cummins), Toyota and Lexus Denso cards and housings (2JZ 22250-46040, 1ZZ/2ZZ, IS F, GR Corolla, GR Supra), Nissan (Z32, the R35/350Z/370Z card 22680-7S000), Subaru, Honda and Acura, BMW, Mercedes, VW, Mitsubishi Karman vortex, and Bosch’s universal HFM-5 and HFM-7 series with the catalogue’s flow ranges and drawing dimensions, plus PMAS HPX and X-MAF, Granatelli, BBK and SCT housings. Each carries its sensor type (card, tube, slot or Karman), wire count, signal type and the vehicles it came on. GM’s placement rule here follows the crate-engine controller sheets word for word: a 4 in tube, the sensor in the middle of a straight section at least 6 in long, the boss centre at least 10 in from the throttle body, the connector between horizontal and straight up, the PCV fresh-air port downstream of the sensor, and a dry filter; an earlier version of this page gave 1 in on the throttle side, which is AEM’s coupler rule, and has been corrected to GM’s 3 in. Ford’s control-pack sheets want the sensor 6 to 8 in upstream of the throttle body and no more than 24 in, in the upper half of the tube, three diameters upstream of the PCV inlet, with the stock tube area kept; any change needs a new PCM calibration. Bosch calibrates element and housing as a unit and says a plug-in sensor’s curve must be determined in the tube it is used in. When the tube changes, every maker asks for a new transfer function; the area ratio new/old is the accepted first guess (HP Academy), then log and correct. NZEFI’s figures for the Nissan card, about 350 hp in a 72.5 mm bore, 500 hp in 85 mm and over 600 hp in 4 in, are a tuner’s test, not Nissan’s. Pro-M, SLP, C&L, Vortech and JLT could not be fetched, and Holley EFI and AEM Infinity run speed-density, so they have no MAF entries.

  • Weld-on MAF bungs and pads. The Parts tab lists 51 weld-on sensor mounts (card pads for the GM LS3/LT card sensor, slot bungs for Hitachi, Denso, Bosch and HPX sensors, Denso round bosses, Ford blade flanges) from ICT Billet, Hawks, Spectre, Ticon, Torque Solution, Wehrli, IAG, VMP, Treadstone, Radium, PRL, CXRacing and others, each with the tube size its underside is coped for and whatever pad size, bolt pattern and placement text the maker publishes. Only ICT publishes a pad envelope (2 × 2 × 1 in and 3 × 2 × 1 in) and only Ticon and VMP a bolt spacing, so most pads are modelled from a guessed 2 in footprint and flagged. Placement follows the makers’ own instructions: Spectre’s kit sheet puts the pad at least 8 to 10 in from the throttle body with the sensor arrow toward it and the PCV hose between the throttle and the sensor; Flowmaster says the centre of 6 in of straight tube, never right after a sharp bend; AEM says the middle of a straight section, to tape the pad on and check fuel trims before welding, and to keep 1 in of straight at coupler ends. The auto-router therefore stands a pad on the middle of the longest straight run, at least 8 in from the throttle, with GM’s 3 in and 1 in straight leads. No maker publishes a rule in tube diameters or a “top of the tube” rule; the forum figure of 10 in from the throttle attributed to GM is hearsay and is not used beyond GM’s own LS guide. The LS3 card sensor is sold by Hawks and Texas Speed in 100 mm (4 in) housings and the pads for it are cut for 4 in (or 3.5 in) tube; ICT notes the sensor is not restricted to a tube size but the ECU then needs a MAF retune. Vibrant, Speed Engineering, Texas Speed, BTR, Mishimoto, Nick Williams and Holley sell no weld-on pad, and JMD Tubes’ MAF flange page could not be fetched; nothing was invented for them. A pad only goes on a naturally aspirated tube or the pipe before the compressor, never on the charge pipe, so the boosted route list leaves it out. Parts with a CAD model tag have a STEP file in the shop’s CAD library folder; the add-in imports it and stands it where the fitting goes (model Y out of the tube, X along it) beside the stand-in, so the real geometry is in the clearance check; SolidWorks part files cannot be imported by the Fusion API and need saving as STEP.

  • Pipe and shell vibration. Span bending modes use the beam formula and end-condition factors for pinned, fixed and cantilever spans (Harvey Mudd notes after Tedesco). Ovaling and ring frequencies use the thin-ring formulas attributed to Den Hartog and Irvine (Eng-Tips), with the ovaling of a long tube in plane strain, E ÷ (1 − ν²) for E (Leissa, Vibration of Shells, NASA SP-288, eqs. 2.22 to 2.27 and section 4.3), and flat panels the simply supported plate formula (SOFiSTiK, after Timoshenko). Room-temperature properties: mild steel 1010 (Elgin), 409 (Combined Metals, Poisson’s ratio assumed 0.29), 304 (Cleveland-Cliffs, Poisson’s ratio from Wikipedia), titanium grade 2 (Aerospace Metals). Stiffness falls with temperature per the ASME B31.1 table (Engineering Toolbox); 409 uses the 12% chromium row and titanium is listed only to 800 °F. Heat growth is expansion coefficient × (wall temperature − 20 °C) × length, with 7.228, 9.9 and 4.8 × 10⁻⁶ per °F for mild steel, 304 and titanium from the material table in the nsxprime “Exhaust Theory” FAQ, and 11.7 µm per m per °C for 409 (0 to 315 °C) from Atlas Steels, which also rates 409 against scaling to 675 °C in continuous and 815 °C in intermittent service. The warning temperatures, 500 °C for mild or aluminized steel and 700 °C for 409, are Potente’s (Acoustics 2005). Slip-joint clearances and the warning about wrapped pipe come from Hugh MacInnes, Turbochargers (HP Books, 1976).

  • Turbos. The turbine changes how low-frequency engine pulses travel on (SAE 2007-01-2205) and turbo builders describe it as acting like a silencer (Vargas Turbo). Treating the turbine as the closed end of the drone check is this calculator’s assumption. Noise types and ranges are from Pai et al., ICSV22 2015. Six full and six splitter blades is a common compressor layout, and top shaft speeds run from about 118,000 to 150,000 rpm on mid-size Garrett GTX units (MotoIQ). Blow-off and bypass valves: EngineLabs. Screamer pipes: Wikipedia. Hugh MacInnes (Turbochargers, 1976) adds that the turbine housing speeds the gas from about 300 ft/s at the port to about 2,000 ft/s, so an oversized turbo manifold gains nothing, that tuned headers on a turbo engine are “more esthetic than power-increasing,” that the pipe right after the turbine should open up fast to break the swirl and can narrow gently after 18 to 24 in, and that twin-turbo manifolds want a balance tube of at least 3/4 in.

Eaton’s TVS rotors have four lobes twisted 160° (Eaton via Autoblog). A screw compressor’s pocket-passing frequency is male rotor speed × male lobes (Turbomachinery Magazine).   • Oval and flat-oval tube. A flat oval’s area and perimeter are exact; an ellipse uses Ramanujan’s perimeter approximation (Wikipedia). Flow and wave calculations use the round tube with the same area, and friction uses the hydraulic diameter, 4 × area ÷ perimeter. Bending stiffness is worked out about both axes. Shell (ovaling) frequencies of oval and flat-oval tube come from a small finite-element ring model, checked against the thin-ring formula for round tube.

  • Pipes made of sections. Each section is a lossless plane-wave transfer matrix with its own area and gas temperature. The resonances are where the pipe responds most between its closed end (valve or turbine) and the open tip, with a 0.6133 × radius end correction at the tip; one uniform section gives the same answer as the quarter-wave formula. Mean flow and wall losses are left out, so real peaks sit a little lower and broader. How tall the peaks are. Each mode now carries its peak height and half-power width from the two losses a lossless chain leaves out: the open tip’s radiation, with the reflection magnitude from Levine and Schwinger’s solution as fitted by Davies (1996, data sheet 3: R₀ = 1 + 0.01336 ka − 0.59079 (ka)² + 0.33576 (ka)³ − 0.06432 (ka)⁴, to ka 1.5; the scan’s last two coefficients are misprinted and the Davies 1988 / Peters 1993 values are used), and the wall’s viscothermal damping α = (1 ÷ ac) √(ων ÷ 2) (1 + (γ − 1) ÷ √Pr) per metre (Rienstra and Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics, 4.5.3 and 5.2.2). The round-trip loss δ = 2 Σ αᵢLᵢ + (1 − R₀) gives the amplification 1 ÷ δ (R&H eq. 5.33 for the wall part) and the half-power width δc ÷ 2πL. Radiation grows as f², wall loss as √f, so the low modes stand tall and narrow and the high ones low and broad; the figures are upper bounds because the engine, the flow and any muffler damp further.

  • How loud, and what to take off. The 4-Stroke tab’s INS reading now gives each run’s absolute level: the open end as a monopole, p = (1 ÷ 4πr) d(ṁ)/dt, so a harmonic of the outflow with amplitude (2/N)|Y| at ω gives ω(2/N)|Y| ÷ 4π pascals at 1 m (the same arithmetic as sound/wam_sound.py, to 0.4 dB on the F-100 run), taken to the roadside distance with 1/r and a hard ground’s +6 dB, A-weighted (IEC 61672) and summed over the orders. With a quiet target it follows Davies’ procedure (Piping system design for low noise, 1996, 3.2 and appendix B): the N orders within 15 dB of the loudest brought to the target less 10 log N each, and the table lists the orders that must fall and by how much, which is the job the Mufflers tab then has to do. No jet noise, no directivity and no surroundings, so it is the order content and a ceiling, not a meter reading.

  • Muffler cut files. The Mufflers tab turns the chamber above into sheet-metal parts: the shell wrap (the inside perimeter at the middle of the wall, by the chamber length plus two plates, for a butt seam), the two end plates and any baffles as a DXF in millimetres on one CUT layer, each plate 0.3 mm under the inside size to slip in, the holes the pipe OD + 0.5 mm, and a tube list with 2 in stubs. A flat-oval case is drawn with the same inside area as the round chamber the tab modelled, at the height you give (W = H + (A − πH² ÷ 4) ÷ H), so the volume built is the volume calculated; a reverse-flow chamber puts both tubes in one plate at OD + 12 mm centres and leaves the far plate blank. The same R12 DXF the hanger and merge-collector files use.

  • Installed attenuation. Davies (Piping system design for low noise, 1996, C.3–C.5 and 2.4) argues that transmission loss between long anechoic pipes “neglects acoustic interaction with other system elements, so is hardly relevant for intake or exhaust design assessments”: what matters is the element with the real tailpipe behind it and the real open end, worked from the termination back. The Mufflers chart has that as a second mode: the tip reflects with Levine and Schwinger’s magnitude and end correction (Davies’ fits), the tailpipe and the element’s transfer matrix carry pressure and volume velocity back to the element’s inlet, and the curve is the fall in the incident wave from inlet to tip. A bare tailpipe gives 0 dB everywhere, a half-wave chamber is transparent, and averaged over tailpipe lengths the installed cut at a chamber’s peak comes back to its transmission loss (9.2 against 9.4 dB in the test); for any one tailpipe the curve swings either side of that, below zero where pipe and element resonate together, which is Davies’ point.
    • 
      
  • Real peak of a side branch. The lossless Helmholtz and J-pipe curves peak at the chart’s cap; the Mufflers tab now also gives the peak at the tuned note for a stated tone level in the pipe, from the quadratic edge loss of the neck or mouth (Rienstra and Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics, 8.3, eqs. 8.24–8.33: a drop of K ρ u|u| ÷ 2 across the opening is, for the first harmonic, a resistance (4K ÷ 3π) ρ u, so at resonance the branch is that resistance alone and the neck velocity solves a quadratic in the incident pressure). With K 2.8 (sharp) and a 150 dB tone a typical can peaks near 20 dB and a J-pipe a little higher; at 130 dB both approach the lossless figure. Neck wall friction is left out. The same K is what the OpenWAM line puts on its loss elements.
    • 
      
  • Books read in full, November 2026. Munjal, Acoustics of Ducts and Mufflers (1987; the extended-tube, reverse-flow and plug elements above, the junction losses of 8.3, the perforate impedances of 3.9); Rienstra and Hirschberg, An Introduction to Acoustics (the wall damping, the grazing-flow whistle of 5.6, the amplitude-dependent neck loss of 8.3 noted for later); Morse and Ingard, Theoretical Acoustics (the chain-of-chambers filter of 9.1, the (1 − M²) flow shift of 11.1, Strouhal shedding of 11.3); Davies, Piping system design for low noise (1996; the open-end reflection fit, the chamber-against-tailpipe rule, his two case studies’ back-pressure numbers); Calton and Sommerfeldt (2017; Ji’s side-branch end correction); Bönnen et al. in Automotive NVH Technology (valve numbers); Bell, Maximum Boost (charge pipes, intercoolers, turbine-inlet pressure); MacInnes, Turbochargers; Vizard, How to Modify Ford SOHC Engines (filters, Tri-Y against 4-1 by cam); Lawlor and Hancock, Auto Math Handbook; Engelman 1973 in the original; Norbye, The Wankel Engine (rotary exhaust duty and temperatures); Howe, Hamilton and Blackstock, Crighton, Kolbrek and Rucz (theses), the Perth College bellmouth thesis (Blair and Cahoon’s Cd fit), the Singh FSAE thesis, and the Samara jet-splitting paper. What each gave the page is cited where it is used; what was read and not used is in docs/research/duct_acoustics_check.md and the reader reports behind it. Smith and Morrison’s Scientific Design of Exhaust and Intake Systems is still unread: the file under that name is Smith and Wenner.
    • 
      
  • Pipes that split in two. With branches, the main pipe runs from the closed end to the split and each branch runs to its own open tip with its own end correction. At the split the branches share the pressure and their flows add, so their admittances add; the resonances are where the closed end sees no flow. The page was checked against the closed-form answer for two identical branches, which act like one branch of twice the area.
    • 
      
  • Gas cooling. With a tip temperature, the gas falls exponentially toward 20 °C between the start and the tip, the shape a pipe losing heat in proportion to its temperature difference gives. Each section, or the whole pipe, uses the speed of sound with the same wave travel time. Pulsating exhaust flow transfers more heat than steady-flow formulas predict (Simonetti et al. 2018), so a measured temperature beats an estimate. For scale, one test of a 1.6 L engine measured 780 K (507 °C) going into the muffler just after the converter at 2,500 rpm and 520 K (247 °C) coming out, and 950 K (677 °C) going in at 5,500 rpm (Liu, Hao and Liu 2012).
    • 
      
  • Catalytic converters. Square cells: pitch = 25.4 ÷ √(cells per in²) mm and open area = (open width ÷ pitch)². Channel loss uses Shah and London’s apparent friction for developing laminar flow in square channels, which Samuels et al. (arXiv 2502.07678) found matches simulations for straight entry, plus entry, exit and cone losses; the power cost is pressure drop × swept volume flow, the pumping work alone. Real engines lose more: in a dyno test of a modified 351 Cleveland at set back pressures (Kevin Davis, quoted in the article “Exhaust Scavenging”), 1.5 psi cost 4% of peak torque and 5% of peak power and 2.5 psi cost 7% of both, from 423 lb-ft and 441 hp. The page interpolates that test as a second estimate and does not extend it past 2.5 psi. A converter quiets the exhaust by reflections at its area changes and by visco-thermal losses in the narrow channels (SAE 2011-24-0219). The channel losses use Stinson’s narrow-tube model (Stinson 1991) with a round channel of the same viscous resistance, and the 1 to 4 kHz figure is a power average. Practical notes on high-flow converters: HP Academy.
    • 
      
  • Boom tubes. Flattening a round tube keeps its perimeter, not its area, so the page works out the width a flat oval needs to keep the area. Friction uses the Haaland friction factor (Wikipedia) with 0.045 mm roughness. The flare recovers full pressure at Jennings’s 8° and none, like a sudden step, at 30° equivalent cone angle; the blend in between is this calculator’s assumption. Jet noise power scales with the eighth power of speed (Lighthill), so at a fixed flow the roar changes by 70 × log of the speed ratio. Panels are simply supported plates between ribs, kept above the firing frequency at redline. Background: EssentiallySports, US patent 6460248.
    • 
      
  • Flex pipes and bellows. Flow over the grooves of an unlined corrugated pipe sheds vortices at a Strouhal number of about 0.25 to 0.38 (frequency × groove width ÷ gas speed), and the whistle locks onto a pipe resonance (Energies 2018, 11, 1954). Gas speed is taken at full throttle with 90% volumetric efficiency.
    • 
      
  • Hangers. The exhaust is treated as one weight bouncing on its hangers: bounce frequency = √(hangers × stiffness ÷ weight) ÷ 2π, and the share of shake passed on follows single-degree-of-freedom transmissibility, which only drops below 1 above 1.41 × the bounce frequency. The soft, firm and polyurethane values (30, 100 and 300 N/mm per hanger) and the damping ratios are typical values chosen inside the 30 to 300 N/mm range an isolator study tested (Atlantis Press); enter your own stiffness if you know it.
    • 
      
  • Stock vehicles. Each preset’s power, torque, RPMs and redline come from the source linked under the picker, and US cars before 1972 carry SAE gross ratings. Where a source gives no redline the page estimates one a little above the power peak and says so. Idle and cruise RPMs are typical values, not factory data. Where a source gives no firing order, the library order for the same layout stands in, which leaves each bank’s pulse spacing unchanged.
    • 
      
  • Street use. California rules are shown only as a reference for street cars: Vehicle Code 27151 and CARB’s aftermarket parts program. They don’t limit anything on the page, which is built for off-road, race and show use too.
    • 
      
  • Fusion panel. Inside the Exhaust Tuner add-in, lengths come from the selected sketch curves or edges, diameters from circular edges and cylindrical faces, bend radii from torus faces, and clearances from Fusion’s minimum-distance measurement. Build this boom tube lofts the inside shape through the page’s sections (round inlet, then flat oval) and shells it outward by the sheet thickness.
    • 
      
  • Cams, mufflers, temperature and flow all move these numbers. Build the primaries or header so they can be adjusted, and measure before you weld the final length.
